claim: Autophagy machinery degrades chloroplast proteins to facilitate efficient nutrient reuse when leaves senesce or experience sugar starvation.
source: When leaves senesce or experience sugar starvation, the autophagy machinery degrades chloroplast proteins to facilitate efficient nutrient reuse.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a summary of the study's context.

claim: Chloroplast budding structures form in sugar-starved leaves.
source: Through live-cell monitoring of chloroplast morphology, we observed the formation of chloroplast budding structures in sugar-starved leaves.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by microscopy data in Figure 1.

claim: Chloroplast buds are released and incorporated into the vacuolar lumen as Rubisco-containing bodies (RCBs).
source: These buds were then released and incorporated into the vacuolar lumen as an autophagic cargo termed a Rubisco-containing body.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through time-lapse imaging in Figures 1-4.

claim: Budding structures did not accumulate in mutants of core autophagy machinery.
source: The budding structures did not accumulate in mutants of core autophagy machinery, suggesting that autophagosome creation is required for forming chloroplast buds.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5 and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Autophagosome creation is required for forming chloroplast buds.
source: The budding structures did not accumulate in mutants of core autophagy machinery, suggesting that autophagosome creation is required for forming chloroplast buds.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that budding structures do not accumulate in autophagy mutants.

claim: Isolation membranes of autophagosomes interact closely with part of the chloroplast surface before forming chloroplast buds.
source: Simultaneous tracking of chloroplast morphology and autophagosome development revealed that the isolation membranes of autophagosomes interact closely with part of the chloroplast surface before forming chloroplast buds.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 6.

claim: Chloroplasts protrude at the site associated with the isolation membranes.
source: Chloroplasts then protrude at the site associated with the isolation membranes, which divide synchronously with autophagosome maturation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 6 time-lapse data.

claim: Chloroplast division occurs synchronously with autophagosome maturation.
source: Chloroplasts then protrude at the site associated with the isolation membranes, which divide synchronously with autophagosome maturation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through time-lapse analysis in Figure 6C.

claim: Autophagy-related division does not require DYNAMIN-RELATED PROTEIN 5B (DRP5B).
source: This autophagy-related division does not require DYNAMIN-RELATED PROTEIN 5B, which constitutes the division ring for chloroplast proliferation in growing leaves.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 8 and 9 showing RCB formation in drp5b mutants.

claim: DRP5B constitutes the division ring for chloroplast proliferation in growing leaves.
source: This autophagy-related division does not require DYNAMIN-RELATED PROTEIN 5B, which constitutes the division ring for chloroplast proliferation in growing leaves.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction.

claim: An unidentified division machinery may fragment chloroplasts for degradation in coordination with the development of the chloroplast-associated isolation membrane.
source: An unidentified division machinery may thus fragment chloroplasts for degradation in coordination with the development of the chloroplast-associated isolation membrane.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion stated in the abstract based on the finding that DRP5B is not required.

claim: Chloroplasts in leaf pavement cells form stromules to activate programmed cell death as an immune response upon perception of an invading pathogen.
source: For instance, chloroplasts in leaf pavement cells form stroma-filled tubular extensions termed stromules to activate programmed cell death as an immune response upon perception of an invading pathogen, in a process regulated by the plant hormone salicylic acid (SA) (Caplan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Caplan et al., 2015).

claim: Stromule formation is regulated by the plant hormone salicylic acid (SA).
source: For instance, chloroplasts in leaf pavement cells form stroma-filled tubular extensions termed stromules to activate programmed cell death as an immune response upon perception of an invading pathogen, in a process regulated by the plant hormone salicylic acid (SA) (Caplan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Caplan et al., 2015).

claim: Stromules are thin, tubular structures of plastid stroma less than 1 µm in diameter.
source: Stromules are thin, tubular structures of plastid stroma less than 1 µm in diameter (Hanson and Sattarzadeh, 2011).
evidence: This is a definition cited from previous literature (Hanson and Sattarzadeh, 2011).

claim: The size and number of chloroplasts gradually decrease when older leaves senesce.
source: When older leaves later senesce, the size and number of chloroplasts gradually decrease (Martinoia et al., 1983; Mae et al., 1984).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Martinoia et al., 1983; Mae et al., 1984).

claim: Autophagy contributes to the decline in chloroplast volume and numbers during leaf senescence.
source: Autophagy is an intracellular degradation machinery that contributes to the decline in chloroplast volume and numbers during leaf senescence (Wada et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Wada et al., 2009).

claim: Core AUTOPHAGY (ATG) proteins (ATG1–10, 12–14, 16, and 18) are highly conserved among plants, yeasts, and mammals.
source: Core AUTOPHAGY (ATG) proteins (ATG1–10, 12–14, 16, and 18) are highly conserved among plants, yeasts, and mammals (Yoshimoto and Ohsumi, 2018; Nakamura et al., 2021a) and are required for the initiation and elongation of the isolation membrane (Nakatogawa, 2020).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Yoshimoto and Ohsumi, 2018; Nakamura et al., 2021a).

claim: Core ATG proteins are required for the initiation and elongation of the isolation membrane.
source: Core AUTOPHAGY (ATG) proteins (ATG1–10, 12–14, 16, and 18) are highly conserved among plants, yeasts, and mammals (Yoshimoto and Ohsumi, 2018; Nakamura et al., 2021a) and are required for the initiation and elongation of the isolation membrane (Nakatogawa, 2020).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Nakatogawa, 2020).

claim: Senescence and sugar starvation preferentially activate piecemeal degradation of chloroplast components involving Rubisco-containing bodies (RCBs).
source: Senescence and sugar starvation preferentially activate piecemeal degradation of chloroplast components involving a specific type of autophagosomal cargo termed a Rubisco-containing body (RCB), leading to smaller chloroplasts (Ishida et al., 2008; Wada et al., 2009; Izumi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Ishida et al., 2008; Wada et al., 2009; Izumi et al., 2015).

claim: Chlorophagy removes entire unnecessary chloroplasts.
source: The second type of autophagy, termed chlorophagy, removes entire unnecessary chloroplasts (Izumi et al., 2017; Nakamura et al., 2018), thereby modulating the number of chloroplasts in a cell (Wada et al., 2009; Izumi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Izumi et al., 2017; Nakamura et al., 2018).

claim: Chlorophagy is likely another form of autophagy termed microautophagy, during which the vacuolar membrane directly participates in sequestering the degradation target.
source: Chlorophagy is likely another form of autophagy, termed microautophagy, during which the vacuolar membrane directly participates in sequestering the degradation target in the absence of encapsulation by autophagosomes (Izumi et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Izumi et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2023).

claim: Plant autophagic bodies and RCBs are typically around 1 µm in diameter.
source: Plant autophagic bodies and RCBs are typically around 1 µm in diameter (Chiba et al., 2003; Yoshimoto et al., 2004), which is smaller than chloroplasts.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Chiba et al., 2003; Yoshimoto et al., 2004).

claim: RCBs are smaller than chloroplasts.
source: Plant autophagic bodies and RCBs are typically around 1 µm in diameter (Chiba et al., 2003; Yoshimoto et al., 2004), which is smaller than chloroplasts.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison based on cited size measurements.

claim: Piecemeal-type chloroplast autophagy via RCBs must start with division of the chloroplast segments that are to be degraded.
source: Thus, piecemeal-type chloroplast autophagy via RCBs must start with division of the chloroplast segments that are to be degraded.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the size difference between RCBs and chloroplasts.

claim: Exogenous application of concanamycin A (concA) allows the vacuolar accumulation of autophagic cargos, including RCBs.
source: Exogenous application of concanamycin A (concA), an inhibitor of vacuolar H+-ATPase, allows the vacuolar accumulation of autophagic cargos, including RCBs, facilitating their visualization (Yoshimoto et al., 2004; Ishida et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Yoshimoto et al., 2004; Ishida et al., 2008).

claim: Many small puncta containing RBCS-mRFP signal accumulated in the vacuole (RCBs) following dark incubation with concA.
source: Following the excision and incubation in darkness of leaves harboring chloroplast stroma–targeted fluorescent protein markers such as RUBISCO SMALL SUBUNIT (RBCS) fused to monomeric red fluorescent protein (mRFP) in the presence of concA, we observed the accumulation of many small puncta containing the RBCS-mRFP signal in the vacuole, that is, RCBs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: This is a direct observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, C.

claim: Addition of sucrose blocked RCB accumulation by rescuing the sugar-starved leaf.
source: Although co-incubation of dark-treated leaves with concA and mineral nutrient–rich Murashige and Skoog (MS) salts did not block the RCB accumulation, the addition of sucrose did, by rescuing the sugar-starved leaf (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: This is a direct observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, C.

claim: No RCBs were detected when leaves of atg7 mutant were subjected to dark incubation in sucrose-free solution.
source: We detected no RCBs when we subjected the leaves of a mutant for the core ATG gene ATG7 to dark incubation in sucrose-free solution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is a direct observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: RCBs are a type of autophagic cargo involved in the degradation of chloroplast fragments in response to sugar starvation.
source: These observations indicate that RCBs are a type of autophagic cargo involved in the degradation of chloroplast fragments in response to sugar starvation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observations that RCBs accumulate in dark-treated leaves but not in atg7 mutants or sucrose-rescued leaves.

claim: Mesophyll chloroplasts form budding structures containing stromal components in dark-incubated leaves.
source: Using dark-incubated leaves from transgenic plants harboring chloroplast-targeted GFP (CT-GFP) or RBCS-mRFP transgenes, we determined that mesophyll chloroplasts form a type of budding structure containing stromal components (Figure 1A, B, arrowheads).
evidence: This is a direct observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: Chloroplast budding structures bud off from their associated chloroplasts within a few minutes.
source: We observed these structures budding off from their associated chloroplasts within a few minutes (Figure 1A, B, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 1A, B and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: The budding structure specifically contains stroma material (EYFP positive) without any chlorophyll signal.
source: Dual detection of the chloroplast stromal marker RBCS fused to enhanced yellow fluorescent protein (RBCS-EYFP) and of chlorophyll autofluorescence confirmed that the budding structure specifically contained stroma material (EYFP positive) without any chlorophyll signal, a marker of thylakoid membrane (Figure 1C, Video 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from dual-channel imaging shown in Figure 1C and Video 3.

claim: Chloroplast buds are cytoplasmic spherical bodies approximately 0.5–1.5 µm in diameter.
source: The chloroplast buds are cytoplasmic spherical bodies (approximately 0.5–1.5 µm in diameter) that are labeled by a chloroplast stroma marker and are adjacent to a main chloroplast body.
evidence: This is a descriptive characterization based on microscopy observations.

claim: Stroma volume decreased in both WT and atg7 leaves after 24 hr dark treatment.
source: After the treatment, stroma volume decreased in both genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The decline in stroma volume was smaller in atg7 leaves (14%) than in WT leaves (30%) after dark treatment.
source: However, the decline in volume was smaller in atg7 leaves (14%) than in WT leaves (30%).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison based on measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The release of chloroplast buds contributes to the decrease in chloroplast stroma volume in sugar-starved leaves.
source: These results suggest that the release of chloroplast buds contributes to the decrease in chloroplast stroma volume in sugar-starved leaves.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that stroma volume decreases more in WT than in atg7 mutants.

claim: TOC64-mRFP signal surrounds a chloroplast bud.
source: Under these conditions, we observed TOC64-mRFP signal surrounding a chloroplast bud (Figure 2A, arrowheads, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Chloroplast buds contain KEA1-mRFP signal but no chlorophyll signal.
source: The chloroplast buds contained KEA1-mRFP signal but no chlorophyll signal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RCBs can be transported with TOC64-mRFP or KEA1-mRFP signal.
source: We also captured the transport of an RCB with TOC64-mRFP or KEA1-mRFP signal (Figure 2B, Video 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Video 5).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 2B, Video 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Video 5.

claim: The budding structures contain chloroplast envelope components.
source: These results indicate that the budding structures contained chloroplast envelope components.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of TOC64-mRFP and KEA1-mRFP signals in chloroplast buds.

claim: No ATPC1-tagRFP signal was detected in chloroplast budding structures, in contrast to the strong stromal RBCS-GFP signal.
source: In the chloroplast budding structures, however, we detected no ATPC1-tagRFP signal, in contrast to the strong stromal RBCS-GFP signal (Figure 2C, arrowheads, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Released RCBs do not contain ATPC1-tagRFP or chlorophyll signals, but accumulate plentiful RBCS-GFP.
source: In agreement with this observation, we captured a released RCB that did not contain any ATPC1-tagRFP or chlorophyll signals, but accumulated plentiful RBCS-GFP (Figure 2D, Video 6).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 2D and Video 6.

claim: Chloroplast buds containing stromal and envelope proteins are released as RCBs without thylakoid membranes.
source: These observations support the notion that the chloroplast buds containing stromal and envelope proteins are released as RCBs without thylakoid membranes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of stromal and envelope markers but absence of thylakoid markers in RCBs.

claim: Live-cell imaging results are consistent with an immuno-electron microscopy study of RCBs in wheat leaves.
source: These live-cell imaging results are consistent with an immuno-electron microscopy study of RCBs in wheat (Triticum aestivum) leaves (Chiba et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature (Chiba et al., 2003).

claim: During the early phase (24.4–34.8 s), the RCB moved rather smoothly in one general direction.
source: A tracking analysis for the RCB indicated that during the early phase (24.4–34.8 s), the punctum moved rather smoothly in one general direction (Figure 3C, Video 7)
evidence: This is a direct observation from tracking analysis shown in Figure 3C and Video 7.

claim: During the later phase (73.8–90.5 s), the RCB appeared to move more randomly, akin to Brownian movement.
source: however, during the later phase (73.8–90.5 s), the punctum appeared to move more randomly, akin to Brownian movement (Figure 3C, Video 7).
evidence: This is a direct observation from tracking analysis shown in Figure 3C and Video 7.

claim: Autophagic bodies accumulating into the vacuolar lumen exhibit random movements.
source: Previous studies showed that autophagic bodies accumulating into the vacuolar lumen exhibit such random movements (Ishida et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Ishida et al., 2008).

claim: The incorporation of RCBs into the vacuolar lumen from the cytoplasm takes place when these structures start to exhibit random movement.
source: We thus reasoned that the incorporation of RCBs into the vacuolar lumen from the cytoplasm takes place when these structures start to exhibit random movement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of movement patterns and comparison to previous studies.

claim: An RCB present in the cytoplasm was engulfed by the vacuolar membrane.
source: From one of our time-lapse imaging series, we identified still frames of an RCB present in the cytoplasm being engulfed by the vacuolar membrane (Figure 4A, open arrowheads from 25.4 to 30.5 s, Video 10).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 4A and Video 10.

claim: The part of the vacuolar membrane that had engulfed the RCB opened, resulting in the RCB being released into the vacuolar lumen.
source: Later in the time series, we observed the opening of the part of the vacuolar membrane that had engulfed the RCB, resulting in the RCB being released into the vacuolar lumen (Figure 4A, filled arrowheads from 47.0 to 52.0 s, Video 10).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 4A and Video 10.

claim: The number of chloroplast protrusions did not increase in atg5 or atg7 leaves during 1-day incubation in darkness.
source: We noticed fewer chloroplast protrusions in dark-incubated leaves treated with concA compared with the respective untreated control leaves, contrary to our hypothesis (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from quantification shown in Figure 5C, D.

claim: The number of chloroplast protrusions did not increase in atg2 or atg10 leaves during 1-day incubation in darkness.
source: We checked single mutants of ATG2 and ATG10 (atg2 and atg10) to investigate other core ATGs and obtained similar results (Figure 5—figure supplement 1): The number of chloroplast protrusions did not increase in atg2 or atg10 leaves during a 1-day incubation in darkness.
evidence: This is a direct observation from quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Autophagosome formation might be required for the production of chloroplast buds.
source: We therefore posited that autophagosome formation might be required for the production of chloroplast buds.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the observation that chloroplast protrusions do not accumulate in atg mutants.

claim: Isolation membranes (marked by GFP-ATG8a) were tightly associated with the chloroplast surface before any budding structure was visible.
source: Following incubation of leaves in darkness and confocal microscopy observation, we observed isolation membranes (marked by GFP-ATG8a) that were tightly associated with the chloroplast surface before any budding structure was visible (Figure 6A, B, 0 s).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 6A, B at 0 s.

claim: The isolation membrane–associated site from the chloroplast side gradually protruded and eventually formed a spherical body containing RBCS-mRFP or CT-DsRed and surrounded by GFP-ATG8a signal.
source: Over time, however, fluorescence monitoring of the same area revealed that the isolation membrane–associated site from the chloroplast side gradually protruded and eventually formed a spherical body containing RBCS-mRFP or CT-DsRed and surrounded by GFP-ATG8a signal, that is, an autophagosome containing an RCB (Figure 6A, B, arrowheads; Videos 15 and 16).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 6A, B and Videos 15 and 16.

claim: The ratio between the major and minor axes of the GFP-ATG8a-labeled autophagosome started to decrease at around 40 s and approached 1 at around 100 s.
source: During this observation period, the ratio between the major and minor axes started to decrease at around 40 s and approached 1 at around 100 s.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from time-lapse data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The chloroplast budding structure appeared at around 50 s and gradually increased in size until around 120 s.
source: The chloroplast budding structure appeared at around 50 s and gradually increased in size until around 120 s.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from time-lapse data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The chloroplast bud appears as the isolation membrane develops and becomes a segmented RCB when the spherical autophagosome forms.
source: These data support the notion that the chloroplast bud appears as the isolation membrane develops and becomes a segmented RCB when the spherical autophagosome forms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation between isolation membrane development and chloroplast bud formation shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The development of the chloroplast-associated isolation membrane precedes the production of chloroplast buds and of RCBs for piecemeal-type chloroplast autophagy.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the development of the chloroplast-associated isolation membrane precedes the production of chloroplast buds and of RCBs for piecemeal-type chloroplast autophagy.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple time-lapse observations shown in Figure 6 and supplementary figures.

claim: 64% of chloroplast buds were GFP-ATG8a positive.
source: Of the chloroplast buds examined, 64% were GFP-ATG8a positive (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: The formation of GFP-ATG8a-labeled chloroplast buds increased in response to the dark treatment.
source: The formation of GFP-ATG8a-labeled chloroplast buds increased in response to the dark treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 3D)
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3D.

claim: GFP-ATG8a-labeled chloroplast buds did not appear in leaves from atg7 plants exposed to dark treatment.
source: but the buds did not appear in leaves from atg7 plants exposed to dark treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3E.

claim: A large portion of chloroplast buds may form synchronously with the development of the isolation membrane under sugar-starvation treatment.
source: Therefore, a large portion of chloroplast buds may form synchronously with the development of the isolation membrane under sugar-starvation treatment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that 64% of chloroplast buds are GFP-ATG8a positive.

claim: 23% of isolation membranes localized on the chloroplast surface as flattened structures.
source: Of the isolation membranes examined, 23% localized on the chloroplast surface as flattened structures (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A, D)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A, D.

claim: 20% of isolation membranes localized with chloroplast buds as spherical or curved structures.
source: and 20% localized with chloroplast buds as spherical or curved structures (Figure 6—figure supplement 4B, D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4B, D.

claim: 43% of the GFP-ATG8a-labeled structures participated in chloroplast degradation during the dark treatment.
source: Therefore, 43% of the GFP-ATG8a-labeled structures participated in chloroplast degradation during the dark treatment in this study.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the sum of percentages (23% + 20%) from Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Chloroplast budding accompanied by autophagosome development substantially contributes to the degradation of chloroplast components in sugar-starved leaves.
source: These results support the notion that chloroplast budding accompanied by autophagosome development substantially contributes to the degradation of chloroplast components in sugar-starved leaves.
evidence: This is an inference based on the quantitative data showing that a significant proportion of isolation membranes and chloroplast buds are associated.

claim: SA might contribute to stromule formation in autophagy-deficient mutants.
source: Since SA signaling stimulates immune responses, including stromule formation (Caplan et al., 2015), we speculated that SA might contribute to stromule formation in autophagy-deficient mutants.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous literature (Caplan et al., 2015) and the observation of SA hyperaccumulation in atg mutants.

claim: Chloroplasts in the guard cells of the atg5 mutant formed more stromules than WT and NahG-expressing plants.
source: Chloroplasts in the guard cells of the atg5 mutant formed more stromules than WT and NahG-expressing plants (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation shown in Figure 7A, B.

claim: The introduction of the NahG construct into the atg5 mutant background (atg5 NahG) largely abolished stromule formation.
source: The introduction of the NahG construct into the atg5 mutant background (atg5 NahG) largely abolished stromule formation (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation shown in Figure 7A, B.

claim: The sid2 mutation resulted in fewer stromules in the sid2 atg5 and sid2 atg7 double mutants relative to the respective atg5 and atg7 single mutants in guard cells.
source: The sid2 mutation also resulted in fewer stromules in the double mutant relative to the respective atg5 and atg7 single mutants in guard cells (Figure 7C, D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation shown in Figure 7C, D.

claim: Many chloroplasts formed stromules in senescent leaves of 36-day-old atg5 and atg7 plants.
source: We next observed stromule formation in mesophyll chloroplasts accumulating CT-GFP or RBCS-mRFP and found that many chloroplasts formed stromules in senescent leaves of 36-day-old atg5 and atg7 plants (Figure 7E, F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation shown in Figure 7E, F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In cells from the third rosette leaves of 36-day-old plants accumulating CT-GFP, stromules were observed in 22.5% or 15.3% of chloroplasts from the atg5 or atg7 single mutants, respectively.
source: In cells from the third rosette leaves of 36-day-old plants accumulating CT-GFP, we observed stromules in 22.5% or 15.3% of chloroplasts from the atg5 or atg7 single mutants, respectively
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from Figure 7E, F.

claim: The introduction of the sid2 mutation in sid2 atg5 and sid2 atg7 led to fewer stromules (9.8% or 2.5% in sid2 atg5 or sid2 atg7, respectively).
source: however, the introduction of the sid2 mutation in sid2 atg5 and sid2 atg7 led to fewer stromules (9.8% or 2.5% in sid2 atg5 or sid2 atg7, respectively; Figure 7E, F).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement shown in Figure 7E, F.

claim: No stromules were detected in the leaves of 20-day-old plants in any genotype.
source: In the leaves of 20-day-old plants, we did not detect stromules in any genotype (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: SA accumulation due to autophagy deficiency activates stromule formation during leaf senescence.
source: These results support the notion that SA accumulation due to autophagy deficiency activates stromule formation during leaf senescence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that reducing SA levels (via sid2 mutation or NahG expression) reduces stromule formation in atg mutants.

claim: In 36-day-old plants, atg5 or atg7 leaves contained 2.7 or 2.8 times more H2O2 than WT leaves.
source: In 36-day-old plants, atg5 or atg7 leaves contained 2.7 or 2.8 times more H2O2 than WT leaves (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The presence of the sid2 mutation in the sid2 atg5 and sid2 atg7 double mutants did not alleviate H2O2 accumulation.
source: Notably, the presence of the sid2 mutation in the sid2 atg5 and sid2 atg7 double mutants did not alleviate H2O2 accumulation (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation shown in Figure 7G.

claim: ROS accumulation may be one factor responsible for the greater number of stromules in sid2 atg5 and sid2 atg7 compared with WT and sid2 plants.
source: Such ROS accumulation may thus be one factor responsible for the greater number of stromules in sid2 atg5 and sid2 atg7 compared with WT and sid2 plants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that H2O2 levels remain high in sid2 atg double mutants despite reduced SA levels.

claim: NahG expression did not counteract the increase in H2O2 level caused by the atg5 mutation.
source: Moreover, NahG expression did not counteract the increase in H2O2 level caused by the atg5 mutation (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: ROS accumulation in atg leaves may not depend on stimulation of SA signaling.
source: ROS accumulation in atg leaves may not depend on stimulation of SA signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that reducing SA does not reduce H2O2 levels in atg mutants.

claim: Many RCBs accumulated when drp5b leaves were incubated in darkness in the presence of concA.
source: Although the mature leaves of drp5b had larger chloroplasts than WT leaves, reflective of the impaired chloroplast division during cell expansion typical of this mutant, many RCBs accumulated when the leaves were incubated in darkness in the presence of concA (Figure 8A, B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation shown in Figure 8A, B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: No RCB was detected in the leaves of the drp5b atg5 double mutant.
source: We detected no RCB in the leaves of the drp5b atg5 double mutant (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: RCB-mediated chloroplast autophagy is active in the drp5b mutant.
source: These results indicate that RCB-mediated chloroplast autophagy is active in the drp5b mutant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that RCBs accumulate in drp5b mutants but not in drp5b atg5 double mutants.

claim: Free mRFP levels increased in leaves of WT but not atg5 or atg7 plants when incubated in darkness without concA.
source: When we incubated the leaves of plants accumulating RBCS-mRFP in darkness without concA, free mRFP levels increased in leaves of WT but not atg5 or atg7 plants (Figure 8C, D)
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 8C, D.

claim: Autophagy-dependent degradation of stromal proteins occurs in response to sugar starvation in WT plants.
source: indicating the occurrence of autophagy-dependent degradation of stromal proteins in response to sugar starvation in WT plants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that free mRFP accumulates in WT but not in atg mutants.

claim: The accumulation of free mRFP in the drp5b mutant was at least as high as that seen in WT plants.
source: The accumulation of free mRFP in the drp5b mutant was at least as high as that seen in WT plants (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The ratio of free mRFP to RBCS-mRFP increased in WT and drp5b plants after dark treatment (6.1 or 4.1 times higher compared with control conditions in WT plants or drp5b, respectively).
source: The ratio of free mRFP to RBCS-mRFP increased in WT and drp5b plants after dark treatment (6.1 or 4.1 times higher compared with control conditions in WT plants or drp5b, respectively), consistent with autophagy-mediated degradation of chloroplast fragments (Figure 8D).

claim: The autophagic degradation of chloroplast stroma is active in both WT and drp5b genotypes.
source: These results indicate that the autophagic degradation of chloroplast stroma is active in both genotypes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that free mRFP accumulates in both WT and drp5b after dark treatment.

claim: The accumulation of free mRFP was 3.2 times higher in untreated leaves of drp5b compared with untreated WT leaves.
source: The accumulation of free mRFP was 3.2 times higher in untreated leaves of drp5b compared with untreated WT leaves (Figure 8D)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The activity of chloroplast autophagy might be constitutively higher in leaves of drp5b than in those of WT plants.
source: therefore, the activity of chloroplast autophagy might be constitutively higher in leaves of drp5b than in those of WT plants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that free mRFP levels are higher in untreated drp5b leaves.

claim: Chloroplast buds were observed budding off in leaves of the drp5b mutant.
source: We observed the budding off of chloroplast fragments in leaves of the drp5b mutant. We incubated a leaf from the drp5b mutant accumulating RBCS-mRFP in darkness, which allowed us to observe the formation of a chloroplast bud and its release (Figure 9A, arrowheads; Video 19).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 9A and Video 19.

claim: In drp5b mutant leaves, vesiculation of a chloroplast fragment starts at the site to which the isolation membranes, labeled by GFP-ATG8a, are tightly associated.
source: In a leaf of the drp5b mutant accumulating RBCS-mRFP and GFP-ATG8a, we detected the vesiculation of a chloroplast fragment starting at the site to which the isolation membranes, labeled by GFP-ATG8a, were tightly associated (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 9B.

claim: DRP5B is dispensable for the autophagy-related division of chloroplast fragments.
source: We conclude that DRP5B is dispensable for the autophagy-related division of chloroplast fragments.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that RCB formation and chloroplast budding occur in drp5b mutants.

claim: Autophagy-related chloroplast division does not rely on DRP5B-mediated chloroplast division.
source: Importantly, we established that the development of the chloroplast-associated isolation membrane and the division of the chloroplast fragment occur simultaneously. This autophagy-related chloroplast division does not rely on DRP5B-mediated chloroplast division.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion based on data from Figures 8 and 9.

claim: The formation of chloroplast buds is unlikely to be linked to the formation of stromules.
source: Likewise, the formation of chloroplast buds is unlikely to be linked to the formation of stromules.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on observations in Figures 5-7.

claim: An unknown division machinery may be required for the autophagy-related division of chloroplast fragments.
source: Therefore, an unknown division machinery may be required for the autophagy-related division of chloroplast fragments.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the finding that DRP5B is not required.

claim: A similar organelle division mechanism takes place during mitophagy in mammals and budding yeast.
source: A similar organelle division mechanism takes place during mitophagy in mammals and budding yeast.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous literature in the Discussion.

claim: The site of a mitochondrion that is associated with the isolation membrane protrudes and divides as the isolation membrane develops and becomes an enclosed autophagosome.
source: The site of a mitochondrion that is associated with the isolation membrane protrudes and divides as the isolation membrane develops and becomes an enclosed autophagosome (Yamashita et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Yamashita et al., 2016).

claim: Mitochondrial division during mitophagy is independent of Drp1 and Dnm1.
source: This type of mitochondrial division is independent of Drp1 and Dnm1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous literature in the Discussion.

claim: In yeast, the mitochondrial intermembrane-space protein mitofissin/Atg44 divides the mitochondrial fragment in coordination with autophagosome maturation.
source: In yeast, the mitochondrial intermembrane-space protein mitofissin/Atg44 divides the mitochondrial fragment in coordination with autophagosome maturation (Fukuda et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Fukuda et al., 2023).

claim: A functionally equivalent protein to mitofissin/Atg44 has not been identified in mammals.
source: A functionally equivalent protein has not been identified in mammals.
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge in the Discussion.

claim: In Arabidopsis plants, ARC6 and PARALOG OF ARC6 (PARC6) mediate the tethering of the FTSZ ring on the chloroplast inner envelope.
source: For instance, in Arabidopsis plants, ARC6 and PARALOG OF ARC6 (PARC6) mediate the tethering of the FTSZ ring on the chloroplast inner envelope (Vitha et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Vitha et al., 2003).

claim: PLASTID DIVISION 1 (PDV1) and PDV2 recruit DRP5B to the division site on the chloroplast outer envelope.
source: PLASTID DIVISION 1 (PDV1) and PDV2 recruit DRP5B to the division site on the chloroplast outer envelope (Miyagishima et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Miyagishima et al., 2006).

claim: The ARC6–PDV2 and PARC6–PDV1 complexes may control the coordination of the stromal FTSZ ring and the cytosolic DRP5B ring.
source: The ARC6–PDV2 and PARC6–PDV1 complexes may control the coordination of the stromal FTSZ ring and the cytosolic DRP5B ring (Wang et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Wang et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018).

claim: The controlled division of plastids requires the cooperation of multiple protein complexes across the inner and outer envelopes.
source: Therefore, the controlled division of plastids requires the cooperation of multiple protein complexes across the inner and outer envelopes.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on cited literature in the Discussion.

claim: Autophagy-related division of chloroplast fragments needs to be carefully regulated, as the size of the segment has to fit into the autophagosome.
source: It seems likely that autophagy-related division of chloroplast fragments needs to be carefully regulated, as the size of the segment has to fit into the autophagosome.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion based on logical reasoning.

claim: The volume occupied by chloroplasts per cell is tightly regulated during cell expansion.
source: Since the volume occupied by chloroplasts per cell is tightly regulated during cell expansion (Pyke and Leech, 1994), the decline of chloroplast volume during starvation or senescence might also be highly controlled.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Pyke and Leech, 1994).

claim: The decline of chloroplast volume during starvation or senescence might be highly controlled.
source: Since the volume occupied by chloroplasts per cell is tightly regulated during cell expansion (Pyke and Leech, 1994), the decline of chloroplast volume during starvation or senescence might also be highly controlled.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on cited literature in the Discussion.

claim: 36% of chloroplast budding structures were not labeled by GFP-ATG8a.
source: In our evaluation of chloroplast buds associated with GFP-ATG8a in excised leaves exposed to darkness (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), 36% of chloroplast budding structures were not labeled by GFP-ATG8a.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Such structures might have formed due to the activities of non-labeled ATG8 proteins.
source: Since endogenous ATG8 family members (ATG8a–8i) were functional, such structures might have formed due to the activities of non-labeled ATG8 proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation in the Discussion.

claim: Autophagy-independent chloroplast budding might occur.
source: Another possibility is that autophagy-independent chloroplast budding might occur.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion.

claim: ATG-dependent pathways were the main routes for the vacuolar degradation of stromal components during the darkness-induced sugar-starvation treatment used in this study.
source: However, biochemical assays for chloroplast autophagy flux suggested that ATG-dependent pathways were the main routes for the vacuolar degradation of stromal components during the darkness-induced sugar-starvation treatment used in this study (Figure 8).
evidence: This is an inference based on biochemical data shown in Figure 8.

claim: CV plays a role in plant responses to abiotic stress, such as drought or salt stress.
source: Previous studies have revealed that CV plays a role in plant responses to abiotic stress, such as drought or salt stress (Wang and Blumwald, 2014; Pan et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Wang and Blumwald, 2014; Pan et al., 2023).

claim: Autophagy, but not CV-dependent pathways, is the main contributor to the adaptative response of metabolism to sugar starvation.
source: A recent study suggested that autophagy, but not CV-dependent pathways, is the main contributor to the adaptative response of metabolism to sugar starvation (Barros et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Barros et al., 2023).

claim: During the early phase of sugar starvation (such as 1–2 days of extended darkness), the autophagy-associated machinery is mainly responsible for chloroplast segmentation and degradation.
source: Overall, these insights support the notion that, during the early phase of sugar starvation (such as 1–2 days of extended darkness), the autophagy-associated machinery is mainly responsible for chloroplast segmentation and degradation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Chloroplast autophagy activity is constitutively higher in leaves of drp5b than in WT plants.
source: An assay of autophagic flux of RBCS-mRFP protein in leaves from drp5b mutants suggested the possibility that chloroplast autophagy activity is constitutively higher in leaves of drp5b than in WT plants (Figure 8).
evidence: This is an inference based on biochemical data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The impaired chloroplast division due to the drp5b mutation might affect photosynthesis-mediated energy production and reduce energy availability, thereby activating chloroplast autophagy without dark treatment.
source: The impaired chloroplast division due to the drp5b mutation might affect photosynthesis-mediated energy production and reduce energy availability, thereby activating chloroplast autophagy without dark treatment.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation in the Discussion.

claim: Mesophyll cells in leaves of drp5b mutants contain few chloroplasts (approximately 4 per cell), whereas those in WT leaves contain approximately 60 chloroplasts.
source: Mesophyll cells in leaves of drp5b mutants contain few chloroplasts (approximately 4 per cell), whereas those in WT leaves contain approximately 60 chloroplasts (Miyagishima et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Miyagishima et al., 2006).

claim: The volume in a cell occupied by chloroplasts is similar between drp5b and WT genotypes.
source: Since the volume in a cell occupied by chloroplasts is similar between genotypes, chloroplasts from drp5b are much larger than WT chloroplasts.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Discussion.

claim: Chloroplasts from drp5b are much larger than WT chloroplasts.
source: Since the volume in a cell occupied by chloroplasts is similar between genotypes, chloroplasts from drp5b are much larger than WT chloroplasts.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the number and total volume of chloroplasts.

claim: Chloroplasts that are too large might show inhibited chlorophagy, resulting in the alternative activation of piecemeal-type chloroplast autophagy.
source: Chloroplasts that are too large might show inhibited chlorophagy, resulting in the alternative activation of piecemeal-type chloroplast autophagy.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation in the Discussion.

claim: Organelle-selective autophagy is typically controlled by receptor proteins that recognize the target organelles and act as a bridge between the organelles and isolation membrane–anchored ATG8.
source: Organelle-selective autophagy is typically controlled by receptor proteins that recognize the target organelles and act as a bridge between the organelles and isolation membrane–anchored ATG8 (Farré and Subramani, 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Farré and Subramani, 2016).

claim: The observation of a chloroplast-associated isolation membrane suggests that the receptors for chloroplast autophagy connect the isolation membrane to the chloroplast envelope.
source: The observation of a chloroplast-associated isolation membrane (Figure 6) suggests that the receptors for chloroplast autophagy connect the isolation membrane to the chloroplast envelope.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations in Figure 6 and general knowledge of autophagy receptors.

claim: Such interaction might facilitate the localization of the isolation membrane on the region of subsequent chloroplast budding and its development along the chloroplast surface.
source: Such interaction might facilitate the localization of the isolation membrane on the region of subsequent chloroplast budding and its development along the chloroplast surface.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion.

claim: In budding yeast, the accumulation of the mitophagy receptor Atg32 is required for the formation of the mitophagosome.
source: In budding yeast, the accumulation of the mitophagy receptor Atg32 is required for the formation of the mitophagosome.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous literature in the Discussion.

claim: Atg32 binds to the mitochondrial outer membrane and interacts with Atg8 and Atg11.
source: Atg32 binds to the mitochondrial outer membrane and interacts with Atg8 and Atg11, the latter being a scaffold protein recruiting other ATG members, for autophagosome formation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous literature in the Discussion.

claim: In fission yeast, Atg43 located on the mitochondrion outer membrane binds to Atg8 to stabilize the autophagosomal membrane for mitophagosome formation during starvation.
source: In fission yeast (Schizosaccharomyces pombe), Atg43 located on the mitochondrion outer membrane binds to Atg8 to stabilize the autophagosomal membrane for mitophagosome formation during starvation (Fukuda et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Fukuda et al., 2020).

source: In mammalian mitophagy, five types of mitophagy receptors have been identified that bind to LC3 (light chain 3) or GABARAP proteins, the mammalian orthologs of ATG8 (Onishi et al., 2021).

claim: Atg39 is the receptor for nucleophagy in budding yeast.
source: Atg39 is the receptor for nucleophagy in budding yeast (Mochida et al., 2015)
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Mochida et al., 2015).

evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Mochida et al., 2022).

claim: The accumulation of receptor proteins might contribute to chloroplast budding to form RCBs.
source: The accumulation of receptor proteins might contribute to chloroplast budding to form RCBs.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion based on analogy to other autophagy systems.

source: PINK1 accumulates on the surfaces of damaged mitochondria, facilitating the ubiquitination of the mitochondria by the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous literature in the Discussion.

source: Five autophagy adaptor proteins have been identified in mammals: p62/Sequestosome-1 (SQSTM1), Next to BRCA1 gene 1 (NBR1), Tax1-binding protein 1 (TAX1BP1), nuclear dot protein 52 (NDP52), and optineurin (OPTN).

source: Another study demonstrated that NBR1 regulates the selective degradation of the outer envelope–bound TOC protein complexes that control cytoplasm-to-plastid protein import (Wan et al., 2023).

source: TOC proteins are ubiquitinated under stress conditions such as ultraviolet-B exposure or high temperature and are then degraded by autophagosomes through NBR1-mediated recognition.

source: Stromule formation is more common in the non-green plastids of tissues without photosynthetic activity than in the mature chloroplasts in leaf mesophyll cells (Ishida and Yoshimoto, 2008; Hanson and Sattarzadeh, 2008).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Ishida and Yoshimoto, 2008; Hanson and Sattarzadeh, 2008).

source: Therefore, the interaction between stromules and the isolation membrane might be important for the efficient degradation of non-green plastids by autophagy.
